intro: Looking for a business visa advisor near you usually means you're planning to come to the UK for business, to work under a sponsored role, or to set up a company here. You want someone local who can explain the rules clearly and guide you through the application. iComply introduces you to a suitable UK immigration adviser who can quote you directly for the help you need.
need_heading: What people searching for a business visa advisor near me usually need
need_lead: Here are the most common situations that lead people to look for a business visa advisor near them.
needs: You are planning a short business visit to the UK and need to understand what activities are permitted without a visa.
You have a job offer from a UK employer and need advice on the sponsored work route and the employer's sponsor licence.
You want to set up a business in the UK and are considering a founder route that requires endorsement.
You are an employer who needs to understand your duties before applying for a sponsor licence.
You need help preparing and submitting an application, or dealing with a refusal or appeal.
context_heading: What to understand about business visa advice
context: In the UK, giving immigration advice is a criminal offence unless the adviser is qualified and regulated. Advisers must be registered with the Immigration Advice Authority (IAA, formerly the OISC) at the right level for your matter, or be a solicitor, barrister or chartered legal executive authorised by their own regulator. You can check the IAA's adviser finder or the SRA register before you share documents or pay.

IAA advisers are registered at levels that limit what they can do, from basic applications to appeals and representation. Ask what level an adviser holds and whether it covers your type of case. iComply is not regulated and does not give immigration advice; we simply introduce you to a suitable professional who can help.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Explain the purpose of your planned UK activity: business visit, sponsored work, setting up a company, or something else.
Say whether you already have an employer or sponsor lined up, or whether you are still exploring options.
Mention any previous applications, refusals or appeals, and any deadlines you are working towards.
Give your current location and where in the UK you need the adviser to be based, if that matters to you.
Describe any specific concerns, such as eligibility for a founder route or sponsor licence duties.
State whether you need help with the initial application, a refusal, or ongoing compliance.
questions: Are you registered with the Immigration Advice Authority, and at what level?
If you are a solicitor or barrister, which regulator authorises you?
Have you handled business visit, sponsored work, or founder route applications before?
What will you need from me to assess my situation?
How will you keep me informed about the progress of my case?
What are your fees, and when will I need to pay them?

faqs.q: Can I work in the UK on a business visit?
faqs.a: No, business visitors cannot work in the UK. A business visit allows certain activities like meetings or conferences, but not employment. If you plan to work, you will need a different visa route, and an adviser can explain the options.

faqs.q: Do I need endorsement for a founder route?
faqs.a: Yes, founder routes need endorsement from an approved body before you can apply. An adviser can help you understand the endorsement process and prepare your application.

faqs.q: Does my UK employer need a sponsor licence?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are coming to the UK for sponsored work, your employer must hold a valid sponsor licence. The employer must apply for the licence and meet certain duties, and an adviser can guide them through this.

faqs.q: How can I check that an adviser is properly regulated?
faqs.a: You can check the Immigration Advice Authority's adviser finder or the SRA register for solicitors. Always confirm the adviser's registration and level before sharing documents or paying any fees.

extra_heading: Choosing between local and remote business visa advice
extra: Searching for a business visa advisor near me suggests you would rather deal with someone you could meet face to face, perhaps because your plans involve documents, signatures or a sponsor who is also local. That instinct is reasonable, but it is worth knowing that many people are advised perfectly well by professionals based elsewhere in the UK, by phone, email or video. The important question is not distance but whether the adviser is regulated for the type of business visa matter you have.

When you compare options, ask each adviser what share of their work involves business visits, sponsored work, global business mobility or founder routes, and whether they regularly deal with employers as well as individuals. If your case involves a sponsor licence, check that the adviser is comfortable advising the employer side too, since the duties fall on the business rather than on you alone. On cost, quotes are price on application, so ask what the fee covers and whether it includes preparing documents, corresponding with the Home Office and any follow-up after a decision.

If meeting in person matters to you, say so when you enquire and give the town or city you can reasonably reach, rather than assuming the nearest adviser is the right fit. A short first conversation usually covers your purpose in the UK, your immigration history, any sponsor or endorsement involved and the documents you already hold. From there the adviser should explain the route that fits, what they would need from you and how they will keep you updated, so you can decide whether to go ahead.

extra_faqs.q: Do I have to use an adviser who is physically near me?
extra_faqs.a: No. What matters legally is that the adviser is properly regulated for your type of case, not how close they are. Many business visa matters are handled remotely, though you may prefer to meet in person for documents or a sponsor meeting.

extra_faqs.q: Can one adviser help both me and my UK employer with a sponsor licence?
extra_faqs.a: Some advisers work with businesses as well as individuals, so it is worth asking whether they can advise on both sides. The sponsor licence duties sit with the employer, so clarity about who is being advised and on what is important from the start.
